title: Each link
hookLine: each generation passes the tradition to the next

lines: MOSES RECEIVED IT, AND HANDED IT ON.
cards: Moses received the Torah from Sinai, and handed it on to Joshua. That's how Pirkei Avot begins, the part of the Mishnah whose name means the Chapters of the Fathers. Not a law, not a blessing, not a wise saying.
It opens with a relay. Joshua hands it to the elders. The elders hand it to the prophets.
The prophets hand it to the men of the Great Assembly. Nobody in that sentence invents anything. Each person does exactly two things: receives, and passes on.
Today's word is the place each of them stands.

teach.b: Tradition calls this line of hands shalshelet ha-kabbalah, the chain of tradition. Look at its two verbs. In Hebrew, Moses kibel, received, and masar, handed over.
Received is a humble word: the Torah came to Moses; it didn't start with him. Handed over is a trusting word: letting go of something precious and putting it into someone else's hands.
Then the Great Assembly speaks, and one of its three sayings is this: raise up many disciples. So the chain was never meant to be a single thread. Each link reaches toward many next links.
The Torah puts the chain somewhere smaller than a school.

In the Shema, Deuteronomy says, "and thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children", and names the places: sitting in your house, walking by the way, lying down, rising up. A kitchen counts. A car ride counts.

teach.h: A RECIPE, A MELODY, A CANDLE.
teach.b: This week the same chain showed up in other forms: a recipe handed down, a melody, a candle lit on the right date, a memory written down so it won't vanish. None of it lasts by being admired.
It lasts by being handed over. And nobody holds the whole chain.
Each link touches the one before it and reaches toward the ones after, and that small reach is the whole job.

how: Pirkei Avot, which opens with the chain from Moses onward, is studied in synagogues and at home, and families pass the tradition on at home: at the Shabbat table, at the Passover Seder, and in stories told to children and grandchildren.

games.q: the chain of tradition — tap the pairs.

s: Pirkei Avot opens with a law
it opens with a relay: Moses received the Torah from Sinai and handed it on to Joshua.
in Avot's first line, Moses receives the Torah rather than starting it
the verb is kibel, received. it came to him, and he handed it over.
Deuteronomy places teaching only in houses of study
it names the house, the road, lying down and rising up.

games.q: you're one of the men of the Great Assembly. the Torah has been handed to you through Moses, Joshua, the elders and the prophets. what do you tell the next generation?
o: guard it closely, and teach only a chosen few.
write it all down, and stop teaching.
games.why: raise up many disciples, one of the Great Assembly's three sayings. the chain was meant to branch, not stay a single thread.

practice: Bring up one story from your family, how two people met, a meal, a mistake everyone still laughs about, in the version that was told to you.
Tell it once in your head, slowly, with the details left in, the weather, the clothes, the exact words someone said, and notice which detail you'd never want dropped.
If you pray, give thanks for the person who handed it to you; if you don't, just hold their name for a moment.

wordCard.voice: Each link. One place in the chain of tradition: a person who receives and hands on, touching the one before and the one after. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: handed over, the verb Pirkei Avot uses for Moses passing the Torah to Joshua.

carryVoice: Your line: receives, and passes on. Every link counts, the kitchen table too. That's plenty for today.
